problemText: Which pronoun is in the subject case? Read the sentence: 'She and Malik carried the heavy box to the car.' Which pronoun does the action, making it the subject?
choices: her
me
she
them
hints: Subject case pronouns do the verb—they perform the action.
Look at the list of subject case pronouns taught: I, we, he, she, they, who.

problemText: Read this sentence: 'Coach gave the medals to the winners and ___.' Which pronoun should fill the blank, and why? Try the drop test by covering 'the winners and' to hear what sounds right.
choices: I
we
us
them
hints: Cover 'the winners and' with your thumb and read: 'Coach gave the medals to ___.'
Remember: object case always follows a preposition, and 'to' is a preposition.

problemText: Two friends are arguing about a sentence. One says, 'The teacher split the supplies between Maria and me.' The other says it should be 'between Maria and I.' Who is correct, and which rule proves it?
choices: The first friend is correct because object case always follows the preposition 'between.'
The second friend is correct because 'and I' sounds more polite.
The first friend is correct because 'I' is always used in pairs.
The second friend is correct because 'between' is a special preposition that takes subject case.
hints: Apply the preposition rule: what comes right after between?
The rule says nothing about politeness—the job the pronoun does decides its case.

problemText: Read this sentence with two blanks: 'Tyler and ___ plan to meet ___ at the park after school.' The first blank needs a subject pronoun, and the second blank follows a preposition. Which pair of pronouns fills both blanks correctly?
choices: me, I
I, me
I, I
me, me
hints: Use the drop test on each blank separately—the same pair does two different jobs here.
For the second blank, identify the preposition 'at' and remember the rule about what comes after prepositions.

problemText: A student wrote: 'Dev and I thanked the coach, and she gave Dev and I a certificate.' This sentence has an error. Identify which blank needs a different pronoun and fix it. What rule solves this problem?
choices: The second blank should be 'me' because pronouns in pairs always need the drop test.
The second blank should be 'me' because it receives the action of the verb 'gave,' making it an object.
The first blank should be 'me' because 'I' is always paired with 'and.'
Both blanks should stay as 'I' because politeness requires subject case in formal sentences.
hints: Cover 'Dev and' in the second blank and ask what is being given: 'she gave ___ a certificate.'
Objects receive the action—they do not do it.

problemText: A student's journal entry contains three pronoun errors to find: '(1) Its important that Kai and me finish the project on time. (2) Between you and I, I think theirs is better than ours. (3) He and him worked together.' Which error is caused by breaking the apostrophe rule for possessive pronouns?
choices: Error 1, because 'Its' should be 'It's' to show the journal belongs to the student.
Error 2, because 'theirs' should be 'their's' when showing ownership.
Error 1, because 'Its' is a possessive pronoun and should not have an apostrophe—it should be 'It's' here, but only because 'It is important,' not because of ownership.
Error 3, because 'him' cannot be used with 'He' in a compound subject.
hints: The apostrophe rule applies to possessive pronouns: its, hers, ours, yours, theirs, whose—none take an apostrophe.
Read error 1 aloud: 'It is important that...' Does the sentence need possession or a contraction of 'it is'?

problemText: An intensive pronoun is used to add emphasis to a subject or object that is already named in the same sentence. Which sentence uses an intensive pronoun correctly?
choices: The coach told myself to run faster.
Herself explained the rules to the team.
We gave the award to ourselves instead of voting.
Maya finished the project herself, without any help.
hints: Remember: an intensive pronoun can be deleted, and the sentence will still be complete with the same subject or object.
Look for a sentence where the -self word emphasizes a subject or object that is already there, not standing in by itself.

problemText: Read this sentence: 'The lifeguard himself spotted the swimmer in trouble.' Use the deletion test to determine whether 'himself' is correct in this sentence. What would the sentence say if you removed 'himself'?
choices: The lifeguard spotted the swimmer in trouble.
The lifeguard himself spotted in trouble.
Spotted the swimmer in trouble.
The swimmer in trouble was spotted by himself.
hints: When you delete an intensive pronoun, the remaining sentence should still be complete and say the same thing.
What subject is 'himself' emphasizing? What does the sentence say without the -self word?

problemText: Which sentence uses 'ourselves' correctly as an intensive pronoun? Remember that an intensive pronoun must have a subject or object already present in the sentence to emphasize.
choices: My sister gave the money to ourselves for the trip.
We baked the entire cake ourselves without using a mix.
Ourselves made a terrible mistake that day.
The team told ourselves to practice harder every day.
hints: Try the deletion test: remove the -self word and check if the sentence still makes sense with the same subject or object.
The intensive pronoun should emphasize a subject or object that is already doing its job somewhere else in the sentence.

problemText: Two sentences are written below. Sentence 1: 'My best friend and myself went to the movie together.' Sentence 2: 'I wrote the entire essay myself without copying anything.' Which sentence has an error, and what is the correct repair?
choices: Sentence 1 is correct; Sentence 2 needs to change 'myself' to 'me.'
Sentence 2 is correct; Sentence 1 needs to change 'myself' to 'I.'
Sentence 1 is correct; Sentence 2 needs to change 'myself' to 'I myself.'
Both sentences are correct as written.
hints: Use the deletion test on both sentences. Which one falls apart when you remove the -self word?
When a -self word is standing in a slot by itself, use the drop test: cover the other name and ask what pronoun that slot needs.

problemText: Read: 'The principal gave the award to the coach and myself at the assembly.' Explain why 'myself' is incorrect in this sentence and write the correct pronoun to use instead. Your answer should identify what job the pronoun needs to do.
choices: It is incorrect because 'myself' can never appear after a preposition; use 'I' instead.
It is incorrect because the word needs to be plural; use 'ourselves' instead.
It is incorrect because 'myself' is standing in the object slot by itself with no other 'me' in the sentence to emphasize; use 'me' instead.
It is incorrect because 'myself' is not as formal as needed; use 'myself alone' instead.
hints: Remember: an intensive pronoun can only emphasize a subject or object that is already present elsewhere in the sentence.
Cover 'the coach and' and read the pronoun alone. What job does that slot need? Is there another 'me' somewhere else for the -self word to point back to?

problemText: Three sentences are listed below. Sentence A: 'The twins decorated the gym themselves, so the decorations looked amazing.' Sentence B: 'Our neighbors told my sister and myself about the surprise party.' Sentence C: 'The winner hugged her parents themselves to thank them.' For each sentence, identify whether the -self word is correct or incorrect. Explain your reasoning using the deletion test or the presence of a subject or object to emphasize.
choices: Sentence A is correct (deletion test passes); Sentence B is incorrect (no other 'me' to emphasize); Sentence C is incorrect (no other subject for 'themselves' to emphasize).
Sentence A is incorrect (no other subject for 'themselves' to emphasize); Sentence B is correct (deletion test passes); Sentence C is correct (deletion test passes).
All three sentences are correct because each contains a reflexive pronoun that refers back to a noun in the sentence.
Sentence A is correct (deletion test passes); Sentences B and C are both incorrect because each uses a -self word in a slot where no other pronoun of the same person is present to be emphasized.
hints: For each sentence, ask: Is there another copy of the subject or object somewhere else in the sentence? Could you delete the -self word and still have a complete sentence?
Remember that the trap is when a -self word stands in a slot by itself, with no other pronoun doing that job elsewhere in the sentence to point back to.

problemText: A writer opens a passage with 'I spent the whole day at the beach with my friends.' Later in the same paragraph, the writer says 'You build sandcastles for hours.' What is the mistake in the second sentence?
choices: The pronoun 'you' shifts to second person, but the passage is written in first person, so it should be 'I' to stay consistent.
The pronoun 'you' incorrectly addresses the reader directly when the passage should maintain focus on the writer's experience using the first person throughout.
The verb 'build' should be changed to 'built' to match the past tense established by 'spent' in the opening sentence.
The pronoun 'you' does not clearly refer to the friends mentioned in the first sentence, making the sentence confusing to the reader.
hints: The lesson teaches that the most common shift swaps person, not number.
Look at who is telling the story in the first sentence, then check if that person stays the same in the second sentence.

problemText: Read this passage: 'My best friend and I joined the soccer team together. We practiced every Tuesday after school. I scored a goal in the game on Friday.' Which sentence contains a pronoun shift, and what should it be changed to?
choices: The first sentence uses 'My best friend and I,' which should be 'We' to match the rest of the passage.
The second sentence uses 'We,' but since only the writer scored the goal, it should be 'I' to match the third sentence.
The third sentence uses 'I,' but since the friend is still part of the team, it should be 'we' to stay consistent.
There is no pronoun shift in this passage because all three sentences describe the same event.
hints: Check which pronouns refer to the same person or group across the whole passage, not just one sentence.
The passage opens with 'My best friend and I,' which is plural. Ask whether a real reason is given for why only one person scored the goal.

problemText: A student wrote: 'I organized my rock collection on Saturday morning. Every rock was sorted by color and size. We placed each one in a labeled drawer.' Is there a pronoun shift? If so, what is the problem?
choices: Yes. 'We' is second person, and the passage is written in first person, so it should be 'I'.
Yes. 'We' is plural, but no second person has been introduced to the reader, so it should be 'I'.
No. The passage correctly shifts from 'I' to 'we' because the student and the rocks are both part of the collection.
No. All the pronouns match because 'we' refers to the student and the collection working together.
hints: Ask yourself: did the passage introduce another person who joined the student to place rocks in drawers?
A number shift happens when 'I' and 'we' get mixed up with no real reason in the story.

problemText: Read this passage: 'My cousin and I built a treehouse all summer long. We nailed boards to the oak tree and added a rope ladder. I cut the wood for the railing while my cousin held it steady. We finished just before school started in September.' How many pronouns shift, and which one sentence contains the pronoun that does not match what the passage already set?
choices: Two pronouns shift: 'I' in the third sentence and 'we' in the fourth sentence both break the pattern.
One pronoun shifts: the 'I' in the third sentence shifts to singular when the passage opens with 'we,' but this is allowed because a real reason is given.
No pronouns shift because the passage correctly shows the two builders working together and then one person doing a solo task.
One pronoun shifts: the 'we' in the fourth sentence shifts back to plural after the passage showed only one person railing.
hints: First, hold the opening pronoun in mind: the passage opens with 'My cousin and I,' which is first person plural.

Check each later pronoun against that opening. The third sentence gives a real reason to shift—one person does one task while the other does another. But does the fourth sentence have a reason to shift back?

problemText: A writer needs to fix this passage: 'I learned to bake cookies at my grandmother's house. She taught me how to measure flour and mix the dough. You have to wait exactly twelve minutes before taking the cookies out of the oven, or they will burn.' Which sentence should be rewritten, and what should the pronoun become?
choices: The third sentence should read 'I have to wait exactly twelve minutes before taking the cookies out of the oven, or they will burn' because the passage is written in first person about the writer's own experience.
The second sentence should read 'She taught me how to measure flour and mix the dough together with you' to introduce the second person pronoun that appears later in the passage.
The first sentence should read 'I learned to bake cookies at my grandmother's house with her help' to explain who the 'you' refers to in the third sentence before it appears.
The third sentence should stay as written because 'you' is an accepted way to give general advice and instructions about waiting for baked goods to finish cooking.
hints: Read the whole passage. Who is telling the story, and what pronoun opens it?
The passage introduces only one narrator learning to bake. Check where the pronoun slides to a different person even though nobody new has joined the story.

problemText: Read this passage carefully: 'My teammates and I practiced our free throws for an hour. We shot from the line over and over until our coach said to stop. Then he asked me to help him carry the equipment to the storage closet. I dragged the heavy box while he held the door open. After that, we celebrated our hard work by getting ice cream together.' How many pronoun shifts occur, which ones are mistakes, and which ones are allowed by the lesson?
choices: There are four shifts total: one allowed shift to 'me' when the coach singles out the writer, one allowed shift back to 'we' when the team reunites, one mistake when 'he' refers to the coach instead of the team, and one mistake in using both 'I' and 'he' in the same sentence.

There are two shifts total: one allowed shift to 'me' in the third sentence because the coach singled out the writer, and one allowed shift back to 'we' in the fifth sentence because the whole team is together again.

There are three shifts total: one allowed shift to 'me' when the coach asks for help, one mistake when 'he' is used instead of 'we' for the coach, and one mistake when 'we' returns in the final sentence.

There are five shifts total: every time the pronoun changes from one sentence to the next counts as a shift, and most of them are mistakes because pronouns should never change within a single passage.
hints: Check whether a real reason is given for each time the pronoun changes. Did the passage explain what happened that would cause a different group to be involved?
The passage mentions at least three different groupings: the whole team, then the writer alone with the coach, then the team again. Ask which shifts are explained by the story and which are not.

problemText: A student wrote this sentence in a math homework assignment: 'I don't have no pencil to write with.' Which choice shows the correct revision for standard English?
choices: I have no pencil to write with.
I do not have any pencil to write with.
I don't have a pencil to write with.
I have not got no pencil to write with.
hints: Standard English allows only one negative word per clause.
When there are two negative words, change one to a positive word like 'any.'

problemText: Read this sentence from a student's draft science report: 'The experiment ain't finished yet, so we can't measure the results.' What verb form should replace 'ain't' in this sentence?
choices: is not
are not
has not
have not
hints: Look at what comes after 'ain't' — 'finished' — to find the helper verb that pairs with it.
'Finished' is a past participle, so you need a helper like 'has' or 'have.'

problemText: A student is writing a thank-you letter to a speaker who visited the class. The draft says: 'Our class don't have words to thank you for your time.' Which revision fixes the subject-verb mismatch for standard English?
choices: Our class is not having words to thank you for your time.
Our classes don't have words to thank you for your time.
Our class does not have words to thank you for your time.
Our class did not have words to thank you for your time.
hints: The subject is 'our class,' which is singular, so find the singular form of the verb.
Match the singular subject 'class' with the standard verb form for 'don't.'

problemText: A student's permission slip says: 'I ain't got no permission slip signed yet.' This sentence has two nonstandard forms. Revise it correctly for formal writing.
choices: I have not got any permission slip signed yet.
I don't have no permission slip signed yet.
I ain't got permission slip signed yet.
I have got no permission slip that is signed yet.
hints: First, replace 'ain't' with the correct helper verb form for 'got' (a past participle).
Then, remove the double negative by changing 'no' to a positive word like 'any.'

problemText: Read this sentence from a school newsletter about a sports day: 'The team captain say she don't think nobody can beat us this year.' Which revision fixes both the subject-verb mismatch and the double negative?
choices: The team captain says she does not think anyone can beat us this year.
The team captain says she doesn't think nobody can beat us this year.
The team captain say she does not think anyone can beat us this year.
The team captain says she don't think anyone can beat us this year.
hints: Match the singular subject 'captain' with its correct verb form.
Change the double negative 'don't think nobody' to use only one negative word.

problemText: A student's draft of a field trip report reads: 'The museum wasn't no place we hadn't never been before, but we was surprised how much there was to see.' This sentence contains three nonstandard forms. After you fix all three for standard English, which sentence below is correct?
choices: The museum is not a place we have never been before, and we were surprised how much there was to see.
The museum was a place we had never been before, but we were surprised how much there was to see.
The museum was a place we had ever been before, but we were surprised how much there was to see.
The museum wasn't a place we hadn't been before, and we was surprised how much there was to see.
hints: Remove both the double negative 'wasn't no' and the triple negative 'hadn't never,' replacing them with single negatives.
Fix the subject-verb mismatch 'we was' and keep the original meaning of the sentence about surprise at the museum.
